lines.text: אבק 10 אגג
tle, seq. עִם. So in Greek, παλαίειν,
συμπαλαίειν, συγκονιοῦσθαι, from πάλη,
κόνις. This rather unusual word seems
to have been chosen by the writer here,
by way of allusion to the torrent יַבֹּק v.
אָבָק m. dust, spec. such as is fine and
light, comp. in r. אָבַק; easily driven by
the wind, Is. 5, 24; or raised by horses
in running, Ez. 26, 10. Hence distin-
guished from עָפָר thick and heavy dust,
Deut. 28, 24. Poet. the dust of God’s
feet, for the clouds, as if trodden of God,
Nah. 1, 3. Comp. שַׁחַק.
אֲבָקָה f. id. whence אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל powder
of the merchant, i. e. aromatic, Cant. 3, 6.
* אָבַר 1. pr. to strive upwards, to
mount, to soar, see Hiph. and the deriv.
אֵבֶר and אֶבְרָה. Perhaps kindr. with עָבַר,
עֲבַר, comp. Pers. ابر eber, ὑπέρ, super, all
which express the idea of above, over,
passing over, transcending; see in עָבַר.
2. Trop. of any force or ἐνέργεια, to be
strong, mighty, see deriv. אָבִיר, אַבִּיר.
Hiph. to mount upwards in flight, to
soar, as the hawk, Job 39, 26.
Deriv. see in Kal no. 1, 2.
אֵבֶר m. a wing-feather, pinion, as the
instrument of flying, soaring, e. g. of the
eagle, Is. 40, 21; the dove, Ps. 55, 7. Dis-
tinguished from the wing itself, Ez. 17, 3.
Poet. ascribed to God, Deut. 32, 11. Ps.
אַבְרָהָם pr. n. Abraham, the founder
of the Jewish nation, son of Terah, born
in Mesopotamia, which he left to wander
through the land of Canaan with his
flocks in the nomadic manner; see Gen.
c. 12–25. In the book of Genesis as far
as to c. 17, 5. he is called אַבְרָם ‘father
of altitude,’ Abram. But in that place,
where a numerous posterity is promised
him, by a slight change of name he is
called אַבְרָהָם ‘father of a multitude,’
(comp. Arab. رُهَامٌ a great number,
multitude,) or as the context explains it
אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם.—So אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם the God
of Abraham, i. e. Jehovah, 2 Chr. 30, 6.
Ps. 47, 10. זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם the seed of Abra-
ham, i. e. the Israelites, Ps. 105, 6. Is.
41, 8. In the same sense simpl. אַבְרָהָם
אַבְרֵךְ a word cried by the heralds
before the chariot of Joseph, Gen. 41, 43.
Were it a Hebrew word, it might be
infin. absol. Hiph. from r. בָּרַךְ, for the
regular הַבְרֵךְ, (comp. אַשְׁכֵּים for הַשְׁכֵּים
Jer. 25, 3,) here supplying the place of
the imperat. i. q. bow the knee; Vulg.
clamante præcone, ut omnes coram eo
genua flecterent; and so Abulwalid and
Kimchi; comp. Lehrg. p. 319.—More
prob. the word is of Egyptian origin, but
changed and inflected by the Heb. writer
so that, although foreign, it might yet
have a Heb. sound, and be referred to a
Heb. etymology; comp. חָם, מֹשֶׁה, פַּרְעֹה.
The true form of the Egyptian word
which lies hid in אַבְרֵךְ, is prob. either
ⲁϥⲣⲉⲕ afrek, i. e. let every one bow
himself, in an opt. sense; so Jablonsky
Opusc. ed. te Water Tom. I. p. 4. Copt.
Vers. John 8, 8; or better ⲁⲡⲉⲣⲉⲕ or
ⲁⲡⲣⲉⲕ, aperek, aprek, i. e. bow the
head, Rossii Etymologiæ Ægypt. s. v.—
See also in אָב no. 7.
אַבְשַׁי see אֲבִישַׁי.
אַבְשָׁלוֹם (father of peace, i. e. pacific)
Absalom, pr. n. a) The third son of Da-
vid, by Maacah, 2 Sam. 3, 3, celebrated
for his rebellion against his father; for
an account of his life and death, see 2
Sam. c. 13–18. As to the sepulchre near
Jerusalem which in modern times has
borne his name, see Bibl. Res. in Palest.
I. p. 519, 520. b) i. q. אֲבִישָׁלוֹם q. v.
* אָגָא obsol. root, Arab. اَجَأَ to flee.
—Hence
אָגֵא (fugitive) Agee, pr. n. m. 2 Sam.
* אָגַג obsol. root, Arab. أَجَّ to burn,
to flame, as fire. Hence the two foll.
pr. names.
אֲגַג and אֲגָג (Num. 24, 7) Agag, pr. n.
of Amalekitish kings, Num. 24, 7. 1 Sam.
אֲגָגִי Agagite, gentile n. of Haman,
Esth. 3, 1. 10. 8, 3. 5. Josephus explains
it by Ἀμαληκίτης. Ant. 11. 6. 5.

line_status.note: The only disagreement is θ vs ϑ in συγκονιοῦσθαι. The typeface's theta is the open, cursive-tailed form (as this 1854 Greek face prints all its thetas), but that is the font's ordinary glyph for the letter theta, not a distinct character; it should be encoded as standard θ (U+03B8), not the compatibility symbol ϑ (U+03D1). Everything else—accents, breathing on παλαίειν, circumflex on οῦ, commas—matches both readings.
Headword vowels: the aleph carries a hataf-patah (two dots plus patah) and the bet a qamets, not patah + shva as in Reading A; the construct אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל is identical in both and matches the print.

Under the ayin the print shows two vertical dots plus a short horizontal stroke — a hatef patah (עֲ), not the T‑shaped qamets of Reading A. This fits the context: line 1 ends with Hebrew עֵבֶר and line 2 opens with the Aramaic/Chaldee עֲבַר. The rest of the line (Persian ابر unpointed, eber, ὑπέρ with rough breathing and acute, italic super, all) is identical in both readings and matches the print.
Printed left-to-right the first item (right after "deriv.") is אָבִיר (qamets, no dagesh) and the second, before the period, is אַבִּיר (patach + dagesh); Reading A reverses them.
Plene spelling: a vav is clearly printed between ל and ם, carrying the holem (לוֹם), not a bare holem on lamed as Reading B has.
After "10" the printed mark is a full stop on the baseline (no descending tail), not a comma — "3, 1. 10." then "8, 3. 5." (Esth. 3:1,10; 8:3,5), matching Reading B.
